practices.title: Gate employee-built software before production
practices.statement: Inventory employee-built automations and prototypes, assign ownership, and route production use through risk-appropriate review for data handling, security, testing, deployment, observability, recovery, and ongoing maintenance.

applicability.description: Organizations where non-engineering staff create AI-assisted automations, dashboards, scripts, integrations, or internal applications.

authoritative_references.title: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework
authoritative_references.supports: Secure software practices need to be integrated into the software development lifecycle to reduce vulnerabilities and their impact.

revisions.reason: The clip usefully distinguishes domain-expert prototyping from production engineering and calls for a shared readiness pipeline. The candidate removes the vendor promotion, fixed 80/20 split, and universal claim that internal staff outperform vendors.
The clip explicitly distinguishes operator-led prototyping and workflow definition from engineering responsibility for hardening, securing, and deploying the system.
The distinction between a fast prototype and a verified, secured, production-operated system directly supports the existing production gate for employee- and AI-built software.

The visual carousel supports treating an AI-built demo as incomplete until security, deployment, observability, recovery, and maintenance concerns receive risk-appropriate production review. Its rigid 13-layer model, 80-percent completeness claim, vendor funnel, and blanket failure predictions are excluded.

practices.title: Engineer AI cost with observable workload evidence
practices.statement: Attribute AI usage and cost by workflow, model, and token class; set budgets and anomaly alerts; benchmark task-specific model routing against quality and latency; and use provider-supported caching only where its semantics, privacy, and invalidation behavior fit.

applicability.description: Applications or teams with metered AI model usage.

authoritative_references.title: GitHub usage-based Copilot billing
authoritative_references.supports: AI-credit accounting across input, output, and cached tokens plus budget controls.

authoritative_references.title: GitHub Copilot usage metrics
authoritative_references.supports: Available usage dimensions and the limits of comparing different reports.

authoritative_references.title: GitHub AI usage optimization
authoritative_references.supports: Provider-specific cache behavior and cost-optimization guidance.

revisions.reason: The reusable practice is measured cost attribution, budget monitoring, benchmarked model routing, and provider-aware caching. It avoids assuming every workflow or provider exposes identical cache semantics or that lower price guarantees equivalent output.

The clip directly supports attributing metered model usage to authenticated users or tiers and enforcing evidence-based spend limits. Its example token allowances and insistence that the gateway rather than application code must enforce every cap are excluded as architecture-specific.

The clip directly supports routing workloads by measured task characteristics and validating quality, latency, and cost for each model tier. Its ten-line implementation, weekly cadence, fixed quality thresholds, named model mapping, and anecdotal savings are excluded.

The clip supports measuring repeated work, benchmarking task-aware model routing, and reducing avoidable request volume. Its named-model recommendations, ten-line classifier, 24-hour cache window, 300-millisecond debounce, 40-to-60-percent hit rate, and 70-percent savings promise are workload- and provider-specific; semantic caching must also preserve authorization, freshness, privacy, and output correctness.

The clip supports evaluating provider-supported prompt caching, asynchronous batch processing for latency-tolerant work, and model routing as cost levers. The catalog candidate correctly requires workload attribution and benchmarking quality and latency instead of presuming discounts preserve outcomes.

The clip supports measuring metered AI spend, caching repeated eligible work, benchmarking lower-cost models for suitable tasks, and setting budgets and alerts. The catalog preserves quality, latency, privacy, invalidation, and provider-semantics checks.

The fixed call-cost arithmetic, 30-to-40-percent savings claim, users-will-not-notice assertion, universal provider-cap claim, and fixed alert and kill thresholds are unsupported or provider- and workload-specific.

The clip supports budgeting for metered AI usage, reducing eligible repeated work, batching latency-tolerant requests, and evaluating smaller models for simpler tasks. The catalog requires workload attribution and measured quality, latency, privacy, and cache semantics.

The fixed cost arithmetic and claims that surviving companies cache aggressively or that unoptimized products fail at month-end are unsupported generalizations. Caching, batching, and model routing depend on correctness, latency, privacy, invalidation, and provider behavior.

practices.title: Gate AI changes with representative evaluations
practices.statement: Keep deterministic assertions for deterministic contracts such as schemas, permissions, tool constraints, and invariants; evaluate variable model behavior against versioned representative datasets and explicit task-relevant metrics; track prompts, models, graders, thresholds, latency, and cost with each result; review borderline or high-impact failures; and continue monitoring the same risk-relevant outcomes after deployment.

applicability.description: Features whose behavior materially depends on probabilistic model outputs, prompts, retrieval, tool use, or model-provider changes.
signals: exact-string output tests, unversioned eval data, unstable graders, or AI releases without production-quality monitoring

authoritative_references.title: NIST AI RMF Core
authoritative_references.supports: Calls for objective, repeatable or scalable test, evaluation, verification, and validation processes with documented metrics and production monitoring.

authoritative_references.title: OpenAI graders API
authoritative_references.supports: Documents machine-evaluable graders and evaluation metrics for model-output assessment.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes the durable need to test non-deterministic output with explicit quality criteria and release thresholds. The candidate corrects its overbroad instruction to replace assertion tests: deterministic schemas, permissions, tool constraints, and invariants should retain deterministic assertions, while probabilistic quality needs representative, versioned evaluations.

The clip independently supports explicit task criteria, regression cases drawn from real failures, and versioned comparisons across prompts and models. Model-as-judge scoring is retained only as one calibrated signal; it should not be assumed accurate or safe enough to replace deterministic checks and human review for high-impact or borderline cases.

The clip independently supports running representative quality evaluations for each model used in routing and comparing quality with latency and cost. The catalog keeps versioned datasets and explicit metrics rather than the clip’s unsupported weekly cadence or universal quality-equivalence threshold.

practices.title: Review AI extensions as supply-chain code
practices.statement: Verify canonical sources and inspect install scripts, hooks, MCP servers, permissions, network calls, updates, licensing, and removal before adoption.

applicability.description: Projects adding third-party skills, plugins, agents, hooks, or MCP servers.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
authoritative_references.supports: External repositories, files, and other content can indirectly alter model behavior; OWASP recommends least privilege, segregation of untrusted external content, human approval for high-risk actions, and adversarial testing.

revisions.reason: Multiple clips expose the surface, but popularity and bundle recommendations do not establish safety.

The clip independently supports periodically reviewing persistent AI configuration for stale, contradictory, or unused instructions and integrations. Its attributed statements, model-update count, universal 90-day purge, and full-stack rebuild cadence are unverified and are not retained as requirements.

The clip proposes agent discovery, evaluation, purchase, and installation without human review. Machine readability can improve evaluation, but it does not establish trust; installation remains a supply-chain decision requiring identity, provenance, permission, network, update, licensing, and removal review.

The clip correctly expands supply-chain review to prompts, skills, shared configurations, and repositories that can alter a tool-using agent's behavior. The catalog practice retains canonical-source, permission, network, update, and removal review rather than trusting a three-tier label.
Recovered current primary-source metadata for the prompt-injection URL already cited by this source revision; the proposition is scoped to untrusted extension content and agent capability controls.

practices.title: Externalize state and checkpoints for long agent tasks
practices.statement: For work that may exceed reliable conversational context, maintain concise durable task state, decompose execution into bounded stages, and validate stage outputs before dependent work proceeds.

applicability.description: Long-running or multi-session agent work with dependent steps, durable decisions, or production impact.

revisions.reason: The clip identifies context drift in long agent work and proposes explicit state, decomposition, and validation checkpoints. The candidate keeps these principles while dropping universal five-to-seven-step chunks, mandatory new sessions, and exaggerated quality claims.
The clip supports decomposing agent work into explicit dependent steps and validating outputs before downstream agents proceed.

practices.title: Distinguish local media processing from API transcription
practices.statement: Document whether captions, frames, video, or extracted audio leave the machine; local tooling does not imply an upload-free workflow when an API transcription backend is configured.

applicability.description: Video/audio understanding pipelines.

revisions.reason: Frame inspection and the Moviola security model distinguish local transforms from optional audio upload.

practices.title: Treat agent memory as governed product data
practices.statement: Separate transient working context from persistent memory; persist only purpose-limited information that improves an approved use case; bind memory to the authenticated user or tenant; record provenance and freshness; apply access controls, retention, correction, and deletion; retrieve only relevant context; and test summarization loss, stale or poisoned memories, cross-user leakage, unsupported recall, and forgetting.

applicability.description: AI assistants or agents that summarize conversations, retrieve prior interactions, or persist user, tenant, workflow, or decision context across sessions.
signals: persistent user memory, conversation summaries, semantic retrieval, or cross-session personalization

authoritative_references.title: NIST Privacy Framework
authoritative_references.supports: Provides a risk- and outcome-based framework for governing personal-data processing across its lifecycle.

authoritative_references.title: NIST AI RMF Core
authoritative_references.supports: Requires privacy requirements, system scope, human oversight, lifecycle risk management, and controls for AI components and data to be defined and documented.

authoritative_references.title: NIST data minimization glossary
authoritative_references.supports: Defines minimization as limiting personal-information processing and retention to what is relevant and necessary for the authorized purpose.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes the useful split between transient context and purpose-specific persistent memory, relevance-based retrieval, selective storage, and recall testing. The candidate adds the missing governance and security requirements: user or tenant scoping, provenance, correction, deletion, and tests for leakage, poisoning, staleness, and forgetting; vector storage is an implementation option, not the practice itself.

practices.title: Validate AI outputs and bound recovery
practices.statement: Define machine-checkable output contracts and policy checks before model output affects users or systems; reject or safely transform invalid responses, bound corrective retries within an overall latency and cost budget, and provide a tested safe failure path such as explicit unavailability or human handoff.

applicability.description: Features that display model-generated content, parse model output, invoke tools from it, or depend on it for user-visible behavior.
signals: blank or unsafe failure behavior after model errors
raw model output reaches users or downstream interpreters without validation

authoritative_references.title: OWASP LLM05 Improper Output Handling
authoritative_references.supports: Recommends validating and sanitizing model output according to context before it is passed to downstream components.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes a reusable runtime control sequence: validate expected structure and limits before display, use bounded corrective retries, and exercise a graceful failure path. The candidate excludes universal two-or-three retry counts, assumes cached or alternate-model fallbacks are safe only when separately validated, and does not treat content filtering as complete hallucination prevention.
The clip explicitly recommends validating agent outputs and making error handling reliable before adding more decentralized handoffs.

practices.title: Manage API compatibility and deprecation explicitly
practices.statement: Define an API compatibility and deprecation lifecycle; version breaking changes using a strategy suited to consumers, publish migration guidance and dates, send standard Deprecation and Sunset metadata where applicable, and monitor remaining use before removal.

applicability.description: APIs with independently deployed or external consumers.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 8594: The Sunset HTTP Header Field
authoritative_references.supports: Machine-readable communication of a resource sunset date.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 9745: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field
authoritative_references.supports: Machine-readable indication that a resource is deprecated.

revisions.reason: The durable practice is an explicit compatibility and retirement lifecycle. The clip is too absolute about path versioning from day one, so the candidate leaves versioning strategy contextual while retaining migration notice, standard metadata, usage monitoring, and controlled removal.

The clip correctly treats an externally consumed response shape as a compatibility contract. The existing practice keeps the useful requirement while replacing mandatory versioning from day one and indefinite v1 stability with a consumer-appropriate deprecation and migration lifecycle.

The clip reinforces treating response shapes as consumer contracts and announcing breaking changes with versions, migration guidance, deprecation warnings, and timelines. The existing candidate preserves that lifecycle while correctly leaving the versioning mechanism and compatibility window contextual.

practices.title: Make automated tests self-contained across environments
practices.statement: Make tests independent of developer-machine residue: validate required configuration explicitly, create and clean isolated data fixtures, avoid order dependence and shared mutable state, control clocks, randomness, and concurrency where they affect assertions, and run critical suites with declared dependency versions and realistic resource constraints; investigate local and CI discrepancies instead of assuming either result is authoritative.

applicability.description: Projects whose automated tests run on developer machines and in continuous integration or other clean execution environments.
signals: tests pass locally but fail in CI

revisions.reason: The clip contributes a coherent cross-environment test-reliability practice: declare configuration, isolate database state, remove test-order dependence, and expose timing or resource-sensitive failures. The candidate also corrects the clip's rhetoric by requiring investigation rather than unconditional trust in one environment.

practices.title: Separate AI-assisted implementation from adversarial review
practices.statement: For critical AI-assisted changes, use an independent review context with explicit abuse, failure, and edge-case goals; investigate disagreements before deployment instead of treating model consensus as proof.

applicability.description: Security-sensitive or otherwise critical code produced or substantially modified with AI assistance.

revisions.reason: At 00:36-02:18 the clip recommends a second model, adversarial review prompts, and rotating builder and reviewer roles. The candidate preserves the useful independence and threat-seeking workflow while excluding unsupported absolutes about model blind spots.

The clip correctly asks for review but directs the same AI workflow to audit its own database, authentication, and API work. For critical layers, self-review alone lacks independence and should be complemented by separate adversarial review and risk-specific tests.

The clip's reusable technical kernel is that AI coding tools still require human direction, judgment, verification, and production hardening. It does not specify an adversarial review method, so this is medium-confidence support rather than a new control.
Transcript and captions directly support human verification before production; the unsourced numerical security statistics are excluded.

The clip reinforces that copied AI-generated authentication and architecture require review rather than trust. Its assertions that identical prompts create identical code, that 10,000 apps share the same vulnerabilities, and that one exploit compromises all such apps are rhetorical and excluded; it offers no concrete review method beyond the existing practice.

The clip supports a human security review before production deployment of AI-generated code. It provides no concrete independent or adversarial review method, so support is limited; the unsourced CVE counts, Carnegie Mellon percentages, 2.7-times comparison, and categorical business-risk claims are excluded.

The clip reinforces reviewing AI-generated changes in a separate PR review step with explicit business-logic, injection, edge-case, query, authentication, payment, and deletion goals before a human merge decision.

practices.title: Document decisions, setup, and failure operation
practices.statement: Keep architecture decision records with context and tradeoffs, maintain reproducible local-setup instructions, and document tested failure-mode runbooks; update each artifact alongside the behavior it describes.

applicability.description: Repositories maintained by more than one person or over a long product lifecycle.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes three reusable documentation surfaces: architecture rationale, reproducible environment setup, and operating guidance for failure modes. The candidate adds lifecycle ownership and tested runbooks; one paragraph per decision and AI-generated playbooks are options, not requirements.
The source treats an owned runbook as a basic production-readiness artifact alongside logging and alerting.

The clip supports writing a calm-state incident checklist covering hosting, database, deploy logs, and rollback. The catalog adds testing and lifecycle updates and excludes the idea that every production incident fits one page.

practices.title: Protect critical branches with review and required checks
practices.statement: Route changes to critical branches through reviewable pull requests and require risk-appropriate status checks before merge; keep changes small enough to diagnose and reverse without assuming every repository needs the same approval policy.

applicability.description: Repositories where changes can reach production or other high-impact environments.

authoritative_references.title: GitHub protected branches
authoritative_references.supports: Documents branch rules that require approving reviews and successful status checks before merge.

revisions.reason: At 00:38-02:13 the clip recommends protected main branches, pull-request review, required automated checks, and small reversible changes. Current GitHub documentation confirms the gating capabilities; the candidate omits unsupported claims that every repository needs one approval or that any particular check would certainly catch a failure.

The clip's per-pull-request preview and required pipeline before promotion support protected merge gates, while the existing practice permits risk-appropriate checks rather than requiring a universal staging topology.

The clip supports protecting the production-bearing branch with tested, reviewed pull requests and keeping feature branches short-lived. Its claims that main is always the deployed artifact, GitHub Flow fits 90 percent of teams, and more complex releases inherently require more long-lived branches are excluded as workflow-dependent.

The clip supports reviewable pull requests, required status checks, and severity-aware merge gating for high-impact changes, while preserving a human decision rather than treating an automated review as proof.

practices.title: Gate changes with risk-based automated tests
practices.statement: Add tests with behavioral changes, cover important success, failure, and abuse paths at the cheapest effective layer, and run a fast required CI suite on every change with broader integration or end-to-end suites at merge or scheduled gates; set coverage and timing thresholds from project risk and evidence.

applicability.description: Projects that can execute automated checks in continuous integration.

revisions.reason: At 00:14-01:30 the clip supports writing tests alongside features, including negative paths, and separating fast unit checks from broader integration tests in CI. The universal 60% coverage floor and categorical push-versus-merge schedule are excluded because appropriate thresholds and gates depend on project risk, test cost, and defect history.

The clip adds concrete support for covering alternate payment methods and representative mobile layouts, not merely the team’s common desktop happy path. Its universal percentages and dollar-loss arithmetic were excluded.

The clip supports treating automated tests and lint as a continuing merge safety net rather than optional work that can be dropped when hosted CI capacity is exhausted. Its fixed team-growth multipliers are illustrative and are not retained.
Selective execution can support risk-based gates, but the claim of unchanged safety requires validated dependency mapping and retained required checks.

The clip supports keeping required checks fast through independent execution and cache reuse where correctness permits. Its claim that a 45-minute pipeline is usually nine serial five-minute steps and its blanket dependency-cache prescription are illustrative, not universal.

The clip supports required automated build and test checks before deployment and retaining version history for diagnosis and recovery. Its yes/no security-vulnerability gate, 30-second rollback promise, and implication that source versioning alone guarantees application rollback are excluded.

The clip supports testing representative device, browser, viewport, and network conditions plus awkward input values and usability observations instead of relying only on the developer’s happy path. The claims that one weakest device proves universal compatibility, that AI never tests these cases, and that exactly five users suffice are excluded.

The clip supports exercising blank and oversized inputs, repeated submissions, phone layouts, error/loading/empty states, and password-recovery paths before calling a demo production-ready. Its universal 30-second usability rule, fixed five-user prescription, and implication that every unexpected action must be crash-proof are excluded.

The visual checklist supports failure-path tests for repeated wrong passwords, nonexistent-account recovery, malformed signup input, and expired sessions before launch. The examples are retained as representative abuse and failure paths, not as a complete security test suite.

The clip supports testing responsive layout, slow-network behavior, error and loading states, offline handling, and frontend performance on representative real devices and connections. Its claims that AI cannot handle these concerns and that UI is the easiest part of every build are categorical and excluded.

The clip supports testing beyond a single local happy path, including crashes and edge cases in the release build before submission. Its rejection certainty and fixed delay claims are excluded because review outcomes and remediation time vary.

The clip supports testing beyond the developer’s machine, account, and happy-path data by exercising representative devices and browsers, awkward input characters, missing data, asset failures, and duplicate submissions. It is a teaser with no testing method, so it supplies supporting examples rather than a new practice; its blanket Safari and uninstall rhetoric is excluded.

The video supports testing realistic non-happy paths before treating a demonstration as production-ready, including unusual input, interrupted navigation, large uploads, and older devices. The weekly frequency, universal user behavior, and claimed financial loss are anecdotal or overbroad and are excluded.

practices.title: Prefer the smallest sufficient change
practices.statement: Surface assumptions, avoid speculative abstractions, and limit edits to behavior required by the current task.

applicability.description: All code changes, including AI-assisted work.

revisions.reason: Two source clips converge on a bounded, auditable coding practice; subjective multiplier claims were excluded.

The clip supports reviewing AI-generated code for comprehensibility, replacing generic names with domain-relevant intent, and removing verified-unused speculative helpers or abstractions. Reading every file aloud, deleting every apparently uncalled function, and assuming smaller code is automatically safer are excluded because reflection, framework entry points, generated code, compatibility, and tests may reveal non-obvious use.

practices.title: Define and verify done
practices.statement: Turn the requested outcome into observable acceptance criteria and run risk-appropriate checks before declaring completion.

applicability.description: Projects containing executable code or configuration.

revisions.reason: Seeded from the understanding and checkpoint workflow synthesis.

The clip independently distinguishes a working prototype from a production-ready product and calls for structured review across security, error handling, deployment, monitoring, recovery, and scope acceptance before customer exposure.

Supports a structured, risk-appropriate review before customers use the system. The catalog retains observable acceptance criteria and targeted checks rather than the clip’s undefined instruction to audit every production layer.

Supports repeatable entry, exit, and pre-release checks rather than relying on exhausted manual review. The catalog requires observable acceptance criteria and risk-specific evidence, not an undefined full-system audit.
The source correctly rejects trusting generated code solely because it came from a newer model and calls for engineering review, hardening, and verification before shipping.
The reusable point is that generated output is not evidence of production readiness; security, compliance, infrastructure, and acceptance checks still require explicit validation.
The source independently identifies verification, security, monitoring, and support as necessary judgment for safely shipping generated software.

The clip supports a repeatable pre-launch review spanning authentication, encryption, session handling, authorization boundaries, rate limiting, input validation, logging, backup, monitoring, and dependencies. Its fixed 47-item enterprise checklist, 90-percent comparison, and claim that most checks need no professional security or engineering input are excluded; checks must be risk-specific and produce observable evidence.

The reusable point is that rapid AI-assisted implementation is not production readiness: architecture, security, testing, deployment, governance, maintainability, and compliance claims require explicit evidence. The clip’s vulnerability and technical-debt statistics, fixed 20-percent framing, death-of-human-development claim, and agency superiority claims are promotional and excluded.

The deploy checklist supports testing in staging and reviewing the diff before production merge. The fixed 30-minute setup promise, guarantee of total confidence, and claim that this prevents every future incident are excluded.

practices.title: Return only the database result shape the feature needs
practices.statement: Select the rows and columns the consuming feature needs while preserving correctness and avoiding compensating round trips or N-plus-one query patterns.

applicability.description: Database-backed application paths where transferred or materialized result data materially affects latency, memory, or network usage.

revisions.reason: The clip identifies unnecessary projections as avoidable work. The candidate is deliberately narrower than a blanket ban on selecting all columns and retains correctness and query-count tradeoffs for later review.

practices.title: Prepare assurance controls and evidence before procurement
practices.statement: Determine which customer assurance artifact and scope is actually required, engage an appropriately qualified assessor early, map the in-scope system and applicable criteria, assign control and evidence owners, operate controls and retain evidence for the examination period, remediate exceptions, and communicate the report type, period, scope, and carve-outs accurately without implying certification or universal coverage.

applicability.description: Service organizations pursuing enterprise customers that request SOC reports, security questionnaires, or comparable independent assurance evidence.

authoritative_references.title: AICPA SOC 2 reporting guide overview
authoritative_references.supports: SOC 2 is an assertion-based examination of a service organization's system description and controls relevant to selected trust services criteria, including control design and effectiveness.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes the durable need to build scoped controls and an evidence trail before a customer procurement deadline. The candidate corrects the clip by making the required artifact, scope, assessor, examination period, and representation contextual rather than treating SOC 2 as universal certification.

The clip supports continuously collecting evidence from operated controls and beginning assurance preparation before procurement pressure. Fixed quarterly reviews, 30-day patching, monthly scans, every successful restore, 60-day Type 1 completion, and six-to-twelve-month Type 2 periods are not universal SOC 2 requirements and are excluded; tools do not replace scoped controls, owners, assessor judgment, or remediation.

practices.title: Operate data retention and deletion as a lifecycle
practices.statement: Inventory data categories and copies, then assign each a documented purpose, authority, owner, access boundary, retention trigger, expiry, deletion or anonymization method, and legal-hold behavior; execute verified deletion requests and scheduled disposal across primary stores, derived data, vendors, logs, and backups while restricting retained exceptions to their permitted use and preserving minimal audit evidence.

applicability.description: Products that store personal, financial, health, tax, contractual, communications, or other regulated or sensitive records.
signals: account deletion, privacy requests, indefinite data retention, regulatory recordkeeping, legal holds, or inconsistent deletion across systems

authoritative_references.title: GDPR Article 17 — Right to erasure
authoritative_references.supports: Article 17 defines grounds for erasure, requires reasonable steps concerning copies when applicable, and preserves scoped exceptions including legal obligations and legal claims.

authoritative_references.title: EU General Data Protection Regulation Articles 5 and 17
authoritative_references.supports: Personal data is subject to storage limitation and erasure rights, with scoped exceptions for legal obligations, public interests, and legal claims.

authoritative_references.title: U.S. Federal Trade Commission: Protecting Personal Information
authoritative_references.supports: Organizations should keep only data needed for legitimate business or legal purposes and maintain a written policy specifying what is retained, its security, duration, and secure disposal.

revisions.reason: The clip correctly distinguishes user-facing deletion from records that may require scoped retention and calls for schedules and audit evidence. The candidate adds purpose limitation, data-copy inventory, legal holds, downstream propagation, backup behavior, restricted use, and verified disposal.

The clip supports treating account deletion as a cross-system lifecycle spanning primary data, backups, analytics, and logs rather than a UI action. The catalog retains lawful exceptions, legal holds, backup handling, vendor propagation, verification, and minimal audit evidence that the clip omits.
The clip usefully treats deletion as a cross-system business process, recommends mapping related records, and calls for automatic lifecycle handling rather than a UI-only delete button.
The clip correctly warns that a privacy promise about deletion is not operationally meaningful if the product and data stores cannot execute it.
Recovered the exact Article 17 reference metadata from this source revision; no practice statement, enforcement state, or new proposition was introduced.

practices.title: Map HIPAA-regulated data flows before applying safeguards
practices.statement: For products that may handle health information, determine whether each organization and data flow is within HIPAA scope; when it is, inventory ePHI across stores, logs, backups, exports, and vendors, implement risk-based safeguards and audit controls, and execute required business associate agreements before disclosing ePHI.

applicability.description: Products used by or for HIPAA covered entities or business associates that create, receive, maintain, or transmit electronic protected health information.

authoritative_references.title: HHS Covered Entities and Business Associates
authoritative_references.supports: Defines regulated entities and when written business-associate arrangements are required.

authoritative_references.title: HHS HIPAA Security Rule summary
authoritative_references.supports: Requires risk analysis, access control, audit controls, transmission security, and reasonable and appropriate safeguards for ePHI.

authoritative_references.title: HHS Business Associates guidance
authoritative_references.supports: Explains when vendors and subcontractors are business associates and the required BAA protections.

revisions.reason: At 00:37-01:43 the clip identifies durable controls: trace protected data beyond the primary database into logs, backups, exports, and vendors; apply access and audit controls; and establish BAAs where vendors act as business associates. The practice first requires a correct scope determination and replaces blanket encryption and vendor-liability claims with current HHS risk-based rules.

practices.title: Track indirect-tax nexus, taxability, and filings by jurisdiction
practices.statement: For cross-jurisdiction sales, maintain a reviewed indirect-tax register that maps nexus indicators, product taxability, registration status, collection configuration, filing and remittance deadlines, and marketplace responsibilities using current revenue-authority guidance or qualified advice; reconcile it to transaction data periodically.

applicability.description: Businesses selling software, subscriptions, digital goods, or services across state or national tax jurisdictions.

authoritative_references.title: California CDTFA Marketplace Facilitator Tax Guide
authoritative_references.supports: Describes registration, collection, filing, marketplace responsibilities, and a current California economic-nexus threshold for taxable merchandise.

authoritative_references.title: California CDTFA use-tax guidance
authoritative_references.supports: Shows that product taxability differs by transaction, including treatment of electronically delivered software.

authoritative_references.title: Texas Comptroller Taxable Services
authoritative_references.supports: Identifies SaaS providers as taxable data-processing-service providers in Texas, contrasting with California treatment.

revisions.reason: At 00:24-01:45 the clip supports reconciling customer locations to nexus rules, configuring collection only where applicable, and tracking filings after registration. The retained practice requires authoritative review and qualified advice; it excludes the unsupported nine-of-twelve-state anecdote, universal thresholds, automatic Stripe sufficiency, and fixed implementation-time claims.

practices.title: Track and satisfy open-source license obligations
practices.statement: Inventory shipped direct and transitive open-source components with versions, provenance, and license identifiers; determine applicable obligations for the actual use and distribution model with qualified review where needed; preserve required notices, source, or other artifacts; and repeat the check when dependencies or distribution change.

applicability.description: Software products and services that incorporate or distribute third-party open-source components.

authoritative_references.title: OpenChain ISO/IEC 5230 license compliance
authoritative_references.supports: Defines key process, role, responsibility, and sustainability requirements for an open-source license compliance program.

authoritative_references.title: SPDX overview
authoritative_references.supports: Defines an open SBOM format and standardized license identifiers and expressions for component inventories.

revisions.reason: The clip adds a reusable requirement to review dependency licenses rather than treating package choice as a security-only concern. The candidate scopes obligations to actual use and distribution and calls for qualified review because license interpretation and remedies are context-dependent.

practices.title: Keep privacy notices aligned with actual data practices
practices.statement: Inventory what personal data the product collects, derives, uses, shares, retains, secures, and deletes; make user-facing privacy representations accurately describe those practices and controls; review the notice and consent flows before launch and whenever data behavior changes; and verify that user choices and deletion commitments work in the product.

applicability.description: Products that collect, use, disclose, retain, or delete personal data and make privacy representations to users.
signals: privacy policy does not match actual collection or deletion behavior

authoritative_references.title: Apple App privacy details
authoritative_references.supports: Requires App Store Connect privacy information for app and integrated third-party code and requires updates when practices change.

authoritative_references.title: Apple App Review Guidelines
authoritative_references.supports: Defines current App Store review criteria, including functionality, privacy disclosures, personal-data sharing, and third-party AI permission requirements.

authoritative_references.title: FTC Privacy and Security business guidance
authoritative_references.supports: Businesses should review privacy policies so they accurately describe practices and honor stated promises.

authoritative_references.title: FTC Privacy and Security Enforcement
authoritative_references.supports: The FTC enforces privacy and security promises and may act when companies mislead consumers or fail to honor representations.

revisions.reason: The clip identifies a durable launch-readiness gap: a copied privacy template that does not describe actual data collection or support promised deletion. The candidate converts that into an inventory, accuracy, change-review, and verification practice.

A visual checklist supports mapping where user data lives and publishing a privacy policy before launch.
