The weekly loop of measuring saves, shares, skips, topics, formats, timing, and direct responses supports iterative post-launch learning. The existing practice supplies the needed outcome orientation and avoids treating one weak result as conclusive.

practices.title: Practice product communication before launch
practices.statement: Develop the ability to explain the problem and product before launch, then use prelaunch conversations and signups as qualitative evidence rather than treating a fixed publishing schedule as proof of demand.

applicability.description: Founder-led products that rely on direct educational or social content for customer discovery and launch distribution.

revisions.reason: The clip recommends practicing video delivery and discussing the product before launch. Fixed 200-day and 100-day countdowns, audience-growth expectations, and causal launch claims are subjective and unverified, so the retained guidance remains promotional advisory only.

practices.title: Bound session replay by privacy and diagnostic purpose
practices.statement: Treat session replay as sensitive telemetry: document the diagnostic purpose and applicable authority, disclose it and obtain consent where required, minimize or sample capture, mask inputs and exclude sensitive workflows, restrict access and retention, verify redaction, and correlate recordings to errors only through protected identifiers.

applicability.description: Products considering session replay, screen recording, rage-click detection, or detailed interaction telemetry
signals: The clip links replay to errors and frustration signals but recommends recording every session without privacy, minimization, masking, retention, or access controls.

authoritative_references.title: EU GDPR Article 5
authoritative_references.supports: Personal-data processing must be lawful, transparent, purpose-limited, minimized, and retained no longer than necessary.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Diagnostic records should exclude, mask, sanitize, or encrypt sensitive data; collection must be legally sanctioned and access and retention controlled.

revisions.reason: Replay can aid diagnosis, but the source recommendation to fully record every session is overbroad and creates privacy and security risk; the candidate retains only a privacy-bounded diagnostic practice.

practices.title: Observe real work before defining product scope
practices.statement: Before defining a solution, observe representative users doing real work, inventory current tools and workarounds, identify frequent or costly workflows and constraints, and validate priorities with multiple users and outcome evidence rather than copying a single customer’s current feature set.

applicability.description: New products, major feature sets, or custom software intended for a target workflow or vertical.

revisions.reason: The useful claim is evidence-led problem discovery and scope discipline. The candidate corrects the clip by requiring representative users and outcome evidence instead of treating one owner’s current software usage as a complete, validated product specification.

practices.title: Preserve in-progress work through reauthentication
practices.statement: When an authenticated session expires, preserve authorized in-progress data and workflow context long enough for the user to reauthenticate and continue without losing work, while applying appropriate privacy, retention, and access controls.

applicability.description: Authenticated workflows where session expiry can interrupt forms, drafts, transactions, or multi-step tasks
signals: The clip explicitly recommends restoring the user to the prior workflow with unsaved form state after reauthentication.

authoritative_references.title: W3C WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 2.2.5 Re-authenticating
authoritative_references.supports: After session expiry and reauthentication, users should continue the activity without losing entered data or context.

authoritative_references.title: W3C Technique G105
authoritative_references.supports: Temporarily retain authorized form data so it can be restored after successful reauthentication.

revisions.reason: The transcript and captions directly support preserving work across reauthentication, and W3C guidance independently confirms the accessibility and continuity requirement.
The clip explicitly recommends preserving authorized workflow state through a failed refresh and returning the user after reauthentication instead of clearing drafts or carts.

practices.title: Detect retention risk from meaningful product behavior
practices.statement: Define meaningful recurring product actions, monitor cohort and user-level changes against appropriate baselines, and test consent-respecting interventions when engagement declines; measure retention and user value rather than treating logins or a fixed inactivity window as proof of churn.

applicability.description: Products where repeat use is a meaningful outcome and behavioral analytics are permitted.

revisions.reason: At 00:48-02:20 the clip recommends tracking meaningful recurring actions, detecting changes from a user’s own baseline, and preparing targeted re-engagement before cancellation. Fixed week-three and three-day rules, the claim that a particular message always works, and unqualified personalization are excluded; interventions must respect consent and be evaluated.

The recommendations for cohort retention, core-action instrumentation, and timely drop-off alerts directly support the existing practice. The catalog statement intentionally replaces the clip's universal three-week and daily-baseline thresholds and automatic email with product-specific baselines and consent-respecting experiments.
The behavior-based retention kernel is reusable, but the clip relies on unsupported fixed windows and conversion percentages, which are not retained.

practices.title: Curate social proof without distorting the evidence
practices.statement: When publishing reviews, testimonials, or social comments as product evidence, use genuine statements in context, preserve their meaning, avoid selection or organization that distorts the overall consumer impression, clearly disclose material connections or incentives, substantiate objective and typical-results claims, and retain source and approval records.

applicability.description: Marketing pages, sales materials, product pages, or campaigns that reuse customer comments, reviews, testimonials, or third-party assessments.
signals: Material connection or incentive is not disclosed
Only favorable reviews are selected in a way that implies representativeness
Published quote cannot be traced to its source and approved wording
Testimonial contains an objective claim without substantiation

authoritative_references.title: FTC ENDORSEMENT GUIDES UPDATE
authoritative_references.supports: The FTC warns that procuring, suppressing, boosting, organizing, publishing, or editing reviews must not distort what consumers think, and material connections require clear disclosure.

authoritative_references.title: FTC ADVERTISEMENT ENDORSEMENTS
authoritative_references.supports: Endorsements must be truthful and not misleading; unrepresentative testimonials can require generally expected results, and material connections should be disclosed.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes the reusable idea of organizing real customer evidence by relevant product, but its advice to curate ruthlessly and collect every public comment omits truth-in-advertising safeguards. The catalog statement preserves context, representativeness, disclosure, substantiation, and traceability so curation does not become deceptive selection.

practices.title: Operate failed-subscription-payment recovery deliberately
practices.statement: For recurring billing, define and test recovery behavior for failed payments: provider-supported retries, customer notification and a safe payment-update path, explicit access and cancellation policy, webhook-driven state reconciliation, and metrics for failure, recovery, support impact, and involuntary churn.

applicability.description: Products that automatically collect recurring subscription or invoice payments.

authoritative_references.title: Stripe Revenue Recovery
authoritative_references.supports: Documents Smart Retries, customer email notifications, recovery analytics, and custom dunning workflows for recurring revenue.

authoritative_references.title: Stripe Automate Payment Retries
authoritative_references.supports: Documents retry constraints, configurable schedules, failure webhooks, and end-state options after recovery attempts.

revisions.reason: At 00:28-01:53 the clip supports treating failed recurring charges as a recoverable workflow with retries, customer communication, and an explicit grace or cancellation decision. The practice makes timing provider- and business-specific and adds state reconciliation and measurement; unsupported fixed 7-14-day schedules, three-email rules, 30-40% recovery, and revenue guarantees are excluded.

practices.title: Give support automation explicit human escalation paths
practices.statement: Automate only bounded, documented support playbooks; escalate low-confidence, contradictory, high-impact, or emotionally sensitive cases to an authorized human with the conversation, customer history, and relevant system evidence preserved, and monitor incorrect closure and escalation outcomes.

applicability.description: Products using AI or rule-based agents to answer or resolve customer support requests.
signals: agents close tickets despite conflicting customer evidence, ambiguous product intent, repeated unresolved issues, or actions outside delegated authority

revisions.reason: The reusable practice is an explicit human escalation boundary for cases where customer evidence conflicts with system state, intent is ambiguous, or broader history and empathy matter. The clip’s universal 70/30 split and claims of perfect playbook execution were excluded.

The clip supports preparing issue-specific support playbooks during feature delivery, distinguishing known bounded resolutions from unknown cases, escalating multi-user, security, and data-integrity incidents, and preserving context for a human decision. Its unsupported 60-70% automation estimate and blanket production-API connectivity are excluded.

practices.title: Make usage billing an auditable event ledger
practices.statement: For metered billing, define billable event identity, account, quantity, unit, occurrence time, and correction semantics; durably record accepted events, deliver them idempotently to the billing provider, reconcile internal totals with provider invoices and entitlements, monitor missing, duplicate, and late events, and retain audit evidence for disputes and adjustments.

applicability.description: Products that charge by usage, credits, API calls, generated artifacts, processed units, or other metered activity.

authoritative_references.title: Stripe record usage
authoritative_references.supports: Documents meter events with customer identifiers, values, timestamps, unique identifiers, and asynchronous processing for usage-based billing.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes the durable requirement to model every billable action as explicit usage data rather than reconstructing invoices from general application logs. The candidate adds idempotent delivery, corrections, reconciliation, and anomaly monitoring; pricing metrics, credits, and one shared table are product-specific choices, and the clip’s churn and ROI claims are not retained.

practices.title: Keep promotional claims out of audit failure criteria
practices.statement: Income, popularity, cost, speed, productivity multiplier, model-superlative, aesthetic, and product endorsement claims remain advisory until independently reproducible and relevant.

applicability.description: Any practice source containing promotional or subjective claims.

authoritative_references.title: SpaceX EU Prospectus dated June 5, 2026
authoritative_references.supports: Discloses the then-proposed Cursor transaction, assets, liabilities, and conditional retention plans; those transaction facts do not establish product quality, infrastructure readiness, or future compensation.

authoritative_references.title: Cursor is now a part of SpaceX
authoritative_references.supports: Confirms completion of the SpaceX acquisition and makes company claims about compute and future products; it does not independently establish engineering quality or hiring and compensation outcomes.

revisions.reason: Consolidated unverified claims so they can never silently become enforced rules.

The claimed delivery-fee percentage, annual savings, custom-build price, universal local demand, and repeatability across every bakery are illustrative sales claims without evidence in the clip; they must not become audit criteria.

The clip’s fixed-cost savings, customer willingness to pay for a sandbox demonstration, negotiation outcomes, and startup-program availability are commercial claims without project-specific evidence. Its replaceable-provider theme is already represented by a narrower catalog candidate.

The claim that one routing decision can halve the bill without changing any output, and the assertion that repeated input necessarily costs ten times more, depend on provider, model, cache eligibility, workload, and quality measurement; they remain promotional until reproduced.

The clip repeatedly claims MCPs are universally obsolete and on-demand integrations are categorically faster and cleaner. Those time-sensitive model-superlative assertions are not independently demonstrated. The useful kernel, minimizing irrelevant loaded tools, is contextual and does not justify an audit failure rule.
Claims that every company will need a new role within five years and that the role will be everywhere are speculative career and market predictions, not auditable project requirements.

The clip is predominantly motivational opinion: it asserts unsupported competitor counts, declares ideas worthless, says a software business model is dead, and promises success from shipping. These are not reusable audit criteria.

The clip universally claims custom software is cheaper, safer from price changes and data use, increases valuation, and will replace SaaS. Those outcomes are context-dependent and unsupported; the useful decision must remain a measured build-versus-buy tradeoff.

The clip presents audience growth, pre-launch trust, referrals, social proof, and selling while building as universal launch requirements without reproducible evidence or project context. These remain commercial hypotheses rather than auditable engineering practices.

The production-database incident is not sourced in the clip, and the recommendation explicitly promotes the creator’s own audit offering. Neither the anecdote nor the vendor claim becomes an audit criterion; only independently supported controls are retained.

The clip's named salary ranges, hiring-company assertions, universal role novelty, and categorical readiness claims are time-sensitive promotional assertions not established by the clip. The security-role descriptions may aid career exploration but are not project audit criteria.

The claims that every business uses 10 to 15 platforms, ignores 950 of 1,000 features, hates its software, needs exactly 50 features, and will become a paying customer are unsupported generalizations. The promises of perfect operation and complete ownership are also excluded.

Claims that humans no longer search for tools, autonomous agent purchasing is the fastest-growing acquisition channel, subscriptions and seats are disappearing, usage pricing is inevitable, and human buyers are leaving are forecasts without evidence in the clip and are not audit criteria.

The transaction and revenue figures are used to infer product quality, infrastructure status, future compensation, and explosive hiring demand, none of which follows from the deal itself. The clip also promotes the creator's courses. These claims remain advisory and are excluded from audit criteria.

The recommendation to publish accurate machine-readable product details may be useful, but the video’s central claims about autonomous AI shopping, guaranteed invisibility, and a permanently changed discovery channel are speculative marketing assertions without project-specific evidence.

The clip markets the creator's engineering audit services while making categorical and unsupported claims about investor NDA behavior, fundability, startup failure, prototyping speed, and code safety. These claims do not establish a reproducible project audit criterion.

Claims that more capable models inherently produce worse architecture, everyone has identical model access, and cleanup demand will explode are unsupported generalizations; they are not enforceable engineering rules.

The 20-percent utilization figure and categorical claims that custom ownership prevents price changes, feature loss, or data misuse—and that all companies are software companies—are persuasive marketing claims rather than reproducible audit criteria.

The clip is a promotional manifesto for AI-directed engineering. Claims that ordinary businesses instantly become software companies with every software-company obligation, that AI replaces an engineering team, that traditional teams cost millions, and that the world added a billion software companies are unsupported and do not define auditable project criteria.

The claims that the test always takes ten minutes and that litigation will take years and substantial money are rhetorical estimates without project-specific evidence; they do not define enforcement criteria.

The worldwide population figures and assertion that lawsuits are exploding are uncited attention claims. Accessibility enforcement should rely on the project's applicable standard and verified conformance evidence, not these figures.
Claims about every model vendor’s original intent, lack of roadmap, and universal absence of quality are unsupported, and the clip explicitly promotes the creator’s branded engineering method.

The clip treats curated endorsements as the only bridge to trust and potentially the most valuable page on a site. Testimonials can inform marketing, but they are selective qualitative evidence and do not establish technical quality, typical outcomes, or an audit failure criterion.

The fixed weekend-versus-three-month narrative and unexplained thirteen-layer audit are creator-specific framing, not reproducible project criteria. The reusable requirements are production gating and risk-based prioritization.

The clip promotes the creator’s proprietary 13-layer production audit and asserts an audit-pen-test-audit sequence is universally required and guarantees procurement success. Those vendor-specific process and sales-outcome claims are unsupported; penetration testing and other assurance activities should be selected from risk and buyer requirements.

The clip uses categorical account-freeze, processor-outcome, and financial-loss claims to create urgency. Current Stripe documentation describes dispute-specific debits, deadlines, reserves, and network monitoring conditions rather than those universal outcomes, so the promotional assertions remain advisory.

The billion-builder figure, claims that no new builder has bad habits, dismissals of coding education, and the branded AI Directed Engineering pitch are promotional generalizations rather than enforceable practices.

The follower, view, interaction, reach, save, share, and zero-spend figures are self-reported promotional outcomes. The claims that free value makes the audience market for you and that reply engagement will be rewarded by the algorithm are not stable or independently established audit criteria.

The clip promotes the creator’s blog and community by contrasting them with named free agent courses. Its claims that 76% of all agent builds fail within 90 days, that the course omits production concerns, and that the creator owns the post-course market are unverified commercial assertions, not audit criteria.

The six-thousand-user scenario and claims that total counts always lie, early detection keeps users, and monthly review loses them altogether are rhetorical. Appropriate metrics and intervention effects must be defined and tested for the product.
The promotional and statistical claims are not independently substantiated in the source and therefore remain non-enforceable.

The lost-laptop scenario, claim that most frameworks default to sessions that live forever, fifteen-device example, and hours-versus-days timeout values are illustrative rather than verified project facts. Timeout and concurrency policy must follow the application's threat model and assurance requirements.

The clip is primarily an advertisement for the creator’s community, certification, and branded curriculum. Its broad point that operating a software business involves non-coding disciplines is not specific enough to create an auditable project practice.
The one-afternoon implementation estimate is promotional and ignores data inventory, policy review, downstream systems, legal holds, access controls, validation, and operational ownership.

The clip is an announcement for the creator’s free community courses and future industry modules. Its descriptions of course coverage and community demand do not supply a project-specific, independently verified engineering control.

The assertions about every endpoint being wide open, technical buyers evaluating APIs first, competitors automatically winning, and APIs being either the biggest liability or most valuable asset are sales framing rather than enforceable criteria.
The source provides no reproducible basis for its quantitative and market-superlative claims; no distinct enforceable implementation practice is established.

Provider pricing, the promise that customers never see a broken feature, and universal one-click immediate rollback are not reliable guarantees. Recovery depends on observability, state compatibility, provider behavior, and tested procedures.
The hypothetical price and productivity claims are not independently reproducible and are excluded from enforcement.

The video promotes the creator's Faction training, mentoring lounge, graduates, certificate, and proprietary thirteen-layer method through an unverified fleet-management success story. It provides no reproducible implementation evidence or audit criterion.

The clip advertises the creator's Faction community, TRI prompts, and companion scripts using unverified audience-demand and copy/paste-to-shipping claims. It offers no reproducible implementation or verification evidence.
The quantitative claims are unsourced and cannot be generalized into audit thresholds.
Costs, quotas, and suitable thresholds vary by plan, workload, runner security, and operations; the exact figures are not enforceable.

Claims that starter platforms fit the first thousand users, migration likely takes two weeks, platforms usually scale further than expected, and slow migration is the most expensive are context-free and not independently evidenced.
The visual slogans are promotional and supply no auditable, reusable engineering claim.

The entire clip markets the Faction curriculum and paid certification program using launch-volume, membership, price, experience, and largest-on-the-planet claims. It provides no project-practice evidence to enforce.
The one-hour access-token assumption is provider-specific, and the claim that nobody else teaches this orchestration except the Faction is promotional and unverified.
The quoted insurance premiums, hypothetical loss, vendor liability examples, and claims about what most builders or underwriters do are context-free and unverified, so they cannot set audit criteria.
The product, ranking, engagement, and pricing claims are promotional and not auditable engineering criteria.

The claims that pricing, permissions, inventory, and account state can never be stale in any system, that testing cannot simulate a thousand concurrent requests, and that better caching is mainly a leadership distinction are categorical and not suitable as enforcement criteria.

The claims that 46% of all new code is AI-generated, AI code has exactly 2.74 times more vulnerabilities, every build receives a security audit, and operators always detect incidents before customers are unverified rhetorical statistics rather than enforceable evidence.

The exact five-minute cadence, guaranteed detection before customers, and money-leak framing are scenario-specific rhetoric; monitoring cadence and alert thresholds must be based on risk, traffic, side effects, and signal quality.

The claims that 90% of scaling problems are connection problems, 80% of database operations are reads, pooling is universally free, replicas necessarily worsen write bottlenecks, and the prescribed order saves thousands are workload- and provider-specific and unsupported.

Calling first-party AI-generated code high trust after line review, claiming no scanning tools exist for community resources, assigning all danger to one tier, forecasting which companies survive, and saying an AI is only as trustworthy as its instructions are unsupported simplifications.

Versioning every API from day one, creating a new version for every response-shape change, guaranteeing version-one clients keep working, announcing every change before shipment, and suggesting an unspecified breaking change may be a lawsuit are categorical or legal rhetoric, not universal audit requirements.

The source is an advertisement for a paid 13-layer audit with fixed price and turnaround promises. It provides no reproducible criteria, methodology, or engineering evidence from which a project practice should be enforced.

The thousand-query, ten-change, 3,500-query, and hourly-change figures are illustrative rather than measured project evidence. Cache-layer and lifetime choices must follow workload, consistency, topology, and cost.

The fixed six-month residue, last-Tuesday data, 200-millisecond timing, every-run race, and categorical claims that CI never lies and local machines do are rhetorical examples. Either environment can be misconfigured; discrepancies require evidence-based diagnosis.

The doubled bill, three-month staging resource, perpetual billing, universal free ingress and paid egress, and 15-percent utilization claims are provider- and workload-specific rhetoric. Actual pricing, commitments, performance headroom, and cleanup safety must be verified before changes.

The claims that a SOC 2 report means controls were found sufficient, every enterprise buyer requires one, deals necessarily stall without it, preparation takes years, and every competitor has already started are inaccurate or unsupported generalizations. Requirements and timelines depend on scope, report type, control maturity, assessor, and customer.

The clip is a product comparison whose claims about Prisma and Drizzle safety, query abstraction, client weight, cold-start speed, optimization responsibility, and production use are version-, runtime-, database-, and workload-dependent. Its useful conclusion is contextual selection, but it supplies no reproducible project evidence or distinct audit criterion.

The source is a launch promotion for the creator’s website, community, downloadable materials, and certification program. It contains no independently reproducible engineering control or implementation evidence suitable for enforcement.

The fixed 00-to-00 cost, millisecond-versus-second latency, categorical claim that images, PDFs, and videos never belong in database columns, and universal requirement that every production system use a URL and CDN are unsupported. Storage and delivery choices depend on object size, consistency, authorization, workload, provider, and lifecycle requirements.

The vendor engine, technology lineage, branching, free-tier, pricing, scale, and production claims are time-sensitive and omit provider- and engine-specific constraints. Database branching does not universally make migrations safe or equivalent to merging code, and the ten-thousand-user threshold is not an architecture criterion.

The clip primarily promotes a three-tier certification by mapping each tier to fixed user-count milestones. Reliability and architecture needs arise from measured workload, risk, and operational context rather than universal counts; the tier-to-scale promises are not reproducible engineering criteria.

The 80-percent traffic, one-schema-per-tenant migration arithmetic, claim of dramatic performance isolation, and assertion that regulated sectors always require a database per tenant are unsupported generalizations. Applicable obligations and customer contracts may require stronger isolation, but isolation remains a spectrum across data, compute, networking, operations, cost, and scale.

Fifteen- or thirty-minute access-token lifetimes are not universal, refresh-token rotation alone does not guarantee a stolen credential is harmless, and vendor defaults can change. Logout and password-change behavior depend on the session architecture; the enforceable requirement is tested expiration, rotation, and revocation appropriate to risk.

The clip is a product comparison with unsupported scale and latency claims and categorical recommendations about pgvector versus dedicated vector databases. Fit depends on retrieval quality, index type, filters, update rate, corpus size, tenancy, availability, backup, operations, and measured workload; 'choose complexity you can defend' is useful advice but not a distinct auditable practice.

One-line middleware, a fixed 60-second lifetime, aggressive caching for most read endpoints, the claim that edge caching means the origin never receives a request, and stacking exactly three layers for instant speed without business-logic change are unsupported. Cache policy must reflect data semantics, personalization, authorization, invalidation, and measured workload.

The universal rule to start every multi-agent system with a central orchestrator and never begin with peer or graph handoffs is unsupported. Topology should follow workflow dependencies, reliability, latency, observability, authority, and cost, with explicit cycle and resource bounds.

The claimed 40-percent cache hit rate, near-zero cached-token cost, 50-percent batch discount, unchanged quality, compounding discounts, and 70-to-90-percent total reduction are provider-, model-, region-, timing-, and workload-specific. 'Cache, batch, tier' is not a universal order and requires measured eligibility and quality.

Never doing any heavy request-cycle work, always responding in 200 milliseconds, particular vendor ease claims, and guarantees of no timeouts or duplicates are not universal. Asynchronous execution adds delivery, retry, ordering, consistency, authorization, storage, and user-state concerns that require explicit design and measurement.

An AI reviewer does not reliably detect every vulnerability, performance issue, logic error, or production failure, and the same model or workflow reviewing its own output is not necessarily independent. Automated findings need validated configuration, human review, risk-specific tests, and false-positive and false-negative measurement.

The fixed 30-day compromise window, zero-downtime and zero-failed-request promises, one-command all-environment swap, and assertion that a manually rotated credential leaves an infinite breach radius are unsupported absolutes. Rotation must be risk-based, provider-supported, and validated in the actual system.

The fixed 13-layer taxonomy, claim that most creators have only two layers, assertion that all remaining layers separate demos from real products, and statement that viewers now know more than 90 percent of peers are unsupported framing. The clip recaps broad topics but supplies no distinct, testable engineering practice beyond candidates already curated from the individual videos.

Claims that most builders have no production visibility, every unhandled exception will be captured, bugs will be found in minutes rather than weeks, and observability alone separates demos from production are unsupported absolutes. Detection depends on instrumentation, sampling, failure mode, privacy controls, alert quality, and tested coverage.

The million-view and million-builder figures, self-reported testimonials about fixing security and scaling, categorical claims that AI-generated code is spaghetti with pervasive bugs and technical debt, and the assertion that this series or branded curriculum bridges projects to production readiness are promotional and not independently reproducible audit evidence.
Recovered primary-source metadata for the two transaction URLs already cited by this promotional revision; the sources contextualize the claims but do not make them audit criteria.

practices.title: Run blameless postmortems and retain the learning
practices.statement: Define postmortem triggers and a reusable template before incidents; after a significant incident, document impact, contributing causes, response, and owned preventive actions without blaming individuals, review the analysis, and retain it in a searchable incident repository.

applicability.description: Teams operating production services where incidents can recur or affect users, data, or availability
signals: The clip recommends a prebuilt postmortem template, prompt scheduling after incidents, systems-focused rather than person-focused analysis, and a shared incident library.

authoritative_references.title: Google SRE: Postmortem Culture
authoritative_references.supports: Postmortems should document impact, causes, resolution, and prevention; remain blameless; be reviewed; and enter a shared repository.

authoritative_references.title: Google Cloud Architecture Framework: Conduct thorough postmortems
authoritative_references.supports: Define postmortem criteria before incidents and conduct blameless postmortems with widely shared outcomes.

revisions.reason: The reusable operational kernel is strongly supported by the transcript, captions, and Google reliability guidance; the source-specific 48-hour deadline is not generalized.

practices.title: Define cache freshness, invalidation, and failure behavior
practices.statement: For each cached datum, define its source of truth, maximum tolerated staleness, cache key and ownership, update or invalidation path, and fail-open or fail-closed behavior; avoid caching security- or transaction-critical decisions unless the consistency contract is preserved; monitor freshness, hits, misses, evictions, and origin load; and test invalidation races, cache outages, cold starts, and stampedes using coalescing, jitter, or other workload-appropriate protections.

applicability.description: Applications using application, database, CDN, client-side, or distributed caches for data whose freshness affects authorization, pricing, inventory, account state, or other business outcomes.
signals: stale pricing, permissions, inventory, and cache stampedes

authoritative_references.title: Redis cache-aside guide
authoritative_references.supports: Cache TTL should match tolerated staleness, writes may require explicit invalidation, and hot misses need stampede protection.

authoritative_references.title: AWS database caching strategies
authoritative_references.supports: TTL choice depends on workload semantics and randomized jitter can reduce synchronized expiry pressure on the origin.

revisions.reason: The clip contributes the durable requirement to define tolerated staleness before adding a cache, own invalidation when source data changes, and plan for stampedes. The candidate replaces categorical zero-staleness examples with explicit consistency contracts and testable failure behavior.

The clip independently reinforces defining acceptable staleness by data type, combining time-based expiry with event-driven invalidation, and preventing hot-key stampedes by allowing one refresh while concurrent callers wait.

The clip independently reinforces explicit invalidation, hot-key stampede protection, and coordinated freshness contracts across CDN, shared cache, and process memory. Its assertion that every wrong-data ticket is usually cache invalidation is excluded as unsupported.

The clip independently reinforces selecting cache candidates from measured request frequency and change rate, choosing the layer and lifetime deliberately, and monitoring hit rate and origin query load after deployment.

The clip supports identifying repeated reads or model calls and choosing browser, CDN, or application caching to reduce origin work. Its advice to cache all expensive-query and AI results, fixed 60-second TTL, 95-percent reduction, and $10-versus-$1,000 comparison are excluded because freshness, key ownership, privacy, invalidation, and workload behavior determine safe caching.

The clip supports selecting cache layers deliberately for shared API responses, edge-deliverable content, and expensive query results, and explicitly mentions invalidating cached results on writes. The existing candidate adds required freshness, authorization, failure, and observability contracts.

The clip supports using cache for repeatedly accessed data to reduce database load. Its instruction to cache the most-accessed data without discussing freshness, key ownership, invalidation, authorization, failure behavior, or stampedes is incomplete; the existing candidate supplies those required controls.

The clip supports avoiding repeated origin reads for suitable reusable data. Its advice to cache anything that does not change every second and its 800-to-50-millisecond and 80-percent-load claims are excluded; freshness, privacy, key ownership, invalidation, outage, and stampede behavior are workload-specific.

The source mentions absence of caching as one possible contributor to growth-related database pressure. It provides no cache selection, freshness, invalidation, privacy, failure, or stampede guidance, so it offers limited support only; caching is not universally required and must follow measured workload evidence and a consistency contract.

The clip supports avoiding repeated computation or database work by caching suitable reusable results. The catalog candidate adds source-of-truth, freshness, invalidation, authorization, failure, observability, and stampede requirements.

Compute once, cache once, and serve fast is not a complete universal strategy; freshness, per-user authorization, key scope, invalidation, eviction, failure, cold-start, and stampede behavior determine whether caching is correct and useful.

practices.title: Test capacity with representative load
practices.statement: Define workload and performance objectives, then test a production-like environment with representative user journeys, data volume, concurrency, steady load, bursts, and relevant dependency behavior; observe latency distributions, throughput, errors, saturation, queueing, and recovery, document safe test boundaries, and rerun after material changes.

applicability.description: Services whose latency, throughput, concurrency, or resource capacity can affect user-visible reliability.

authoritative_references.title: AWS performance testing guidance
authoritative_references.supports: Defines load, stress, and scalability testing against production-like environments and measured historical baselines.

authoritative_references.title: Microsoft Azure performance testing guidance
authoritative_references.supports: Requires representative conditions, production-like configurations, progressive load, observed latency, throughput, errors, and resource use, with explicit production-test risk controls.

revisions.reason: The clip directly supports simulated traffic before launch to discover scaling bottlenecks. The candidate turns that into measurable workload objectives, representative environments and journeys, multiple load shapes, diagnostic signals, safe boundaries, and repeat testing after material changes.

The fixed ten-, hundred-, and thousand-user cliff, query timings, and assertion that AI-generated code is designed only to work are illustrative rather than general. Capacity depends on workload shape, data, dependencies, infrastructure, objectives, and observed bottlenecks.

practices.title: Design downstream change propagation as replayable delivery
practices.statement: Choose CDC, an outbox, or another synchronization mechanism from the consistency and latency contract; publish versioned minimal events, make consumers idempotent, monitor lag and failures, and provide bounded retry, dead-letter inspection, and tested replay or reconciliation.

applicability.description: Systems that propagate database changes to indexes, analytics, notifications, caches, or other downstream consumers.
