practices.title: Monitor critical user journeys end to end
practices.statement: Define a small set of user- and business-relevant indicators for critical journeys, instrument each outcome, and run safe synthetic checks where appropriate; alert on actionable divergence between infrastructure health and journey success, then preserve enough step-level evidence to diagnose failures.

applicability.description: Products with critical multi-step journeys such as signup, checkout, payment, fulfillment, or credential issuance.
signals: healthy infrastructure but failed business outcome

authoritative_references.title: Google SRE Service Level Objectives
authoritative_references.supports: SLIs should represent user-relevant service behavior, including correctness, and may require client-side or black-box measurement.

authoritative_references.title: Google Cloud synthetic monitoring
authoritative_references.supports: Synthetic monitors test service, application, page, and API availability, consistency, and performance.

revisions.reason: The clip supports monitoring business outcomes separately from server health and exercising a critical path synthetically. The five-minute cadence and payments-per-hour examples are not universal; frequency, test accounts, cost, privacy, and side effects must fit the product.

The failed-payment example independently supports user- and business-relevant indicators and actionable alerts when infrastructure health diverges from checkout outcomes. Fixed claims about customer loss, word of mouth, fees, and discovery being the single most expensive variable are excluded as unsupported and non-universal.
The source directly supports user-visible synthetic monitoring; multiple regions are appropriate where reachability risk and user geography justify them.
The source strongly supports monitoring the end-to-end business outcome rather than relying on generic error and behavior dashboards.
The clip correctly separates business-outcome indicators from infrastructure health and recommends safe synthetic exercise of the signup-to-payment path so silent journey failures become alertable.

The clip independently supports combining basic liveness checks, exception evidence, and external multi-region monitoring so teams detect failures before customers report them. Its fixed 60-second cadence, ten-minute setup promise, and instant-phone escalation are excluded because alert timing and routing must follow service objectives and operational context.

practices.title: Separate webhook acceptance from business processing
practices.statement: Verify and durably accept required webhook events before acknowledging delivery, process them asynchronously and idempotently, track accepted, processed, failed, and reconciled states separately, and provide retries, dead-letter inspection, alerts, and provider-state reconciliation for business-critical events.

applicability.description: Business-critical webhook integrations for payments, subscriptions, fulfillment, identity, or other external state changes
signals: The clip shows how a transport-level 2xx can conceal failed business processing when acceptance and downstream outcome are not monitored separately.

authoritative_references.title: Stripe Docs: Receive events in your webhook endpoint
authoritative_references.supports: Stripe recommends signature-aware handlers, asynchronous queues, duplicate handling, and a quick 2xx before complex downstream logic.

authoritative_references.title: Stripe Docs: Process undelivered webhook events
authoritative_references.supports: Stripe documents retries, idempotent processing, processed-state tracking, and manual recovery for undelivered events.

revisions.reason: The source correctly identifies silent business-processing failure but incorrectly implies that all downstream work should finish before a 2xx; the candidate uses durable acceptance plus independently monitored asynchronous processing.

A dead-letter queue does not automatically detect that arbitrary business logic produced a wrong outcome after an HTTP 200. The durable pattern is verified acceptance, explicit accepted/processed/failed state, idempotent processing, bounded retries, DLQ inspection, and provider reconciliation.

practices.title: Escalate authentication when risk changes
practices.statement: Use relevant, privacy-reviewed risk signals to trigger step-up authentication or protective action for sensitive operations and material session changes; do not treat network location alone as trust.

applicability.description: Authenticated applications with sensitive operations and a threat model that justifies adaptive or risk-based authentication.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Adaptive authentication may require different authentication stages based on contextual attributes and operation sensitivity.

authoritative_references.title: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture
authoritative_references.supports: Zero trust grants no implicit trust based solely on network location or asset ownership and protects resources through authentication and authorization.

revisions.reason: The clip supports contextual step-up authentication and rejection of perimeter-based implicit trust. The candidate avoids requiring continuous scoring or denial on any single signal because signal quality, privacy, spoofability, and recovery paths require threat-model-specific design.

practices.title: Bound AI-agent capabilities with enforceable controls
practices.statement: Give agents distinct task-scoped identities, least-privilege tools and short-lived credentials, explicit resource and egress limits, and policy gates for high-impact actions; log security-relevant tool calls and approvals in protected audit records, then test denial paths before production.

applicability.description: AI agents that can call tools, access private data, change systems, or communicate externally.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency
authoritative_references.supports: Minimizing agent functionality and permissions plus logging and monitoring downstream actions.

authoritative_references.title: NIST SP 800-171r3
authoritative_references.supports: Least privilege for system processes and protection, retention, and review of security audit records.

authoritative_references.title: NIST AI RMF Measure Playbook
authoritative_references.supports: Auditability, range-violation logging, human-oversight measurement, and production monitoring.

revisions.reason: The durable control is enforceable least agency, not a reviewer clicking approve. The candidate narrows access before execution, protects security-relevant logs without requiring sensitive chain-of-thought capture, and requires tests proving prohibited actions are denied.

The clip usefully keeps humans in the loop for unknown or consequential support cases, but its advice to connect an agent to every production API and let it execute after a generic human decision conflicts with task-scoped least privilege and action-specific policy gates.

practices.title: Treat agent context as untrusted input
practices.statement: Treat repository content, issues, documents, retrieved pages, tool responses, and other externally influenced agent context as untrusted data; identify and segregate it from instructions, constrain agent privileges, require approval for high-impact actions, keep tooling patched, and adversarially test indirect prompt-injection paths.

applicability.description: AI coding assistants or agents that ingest externally influenced content and can execute tools or modify developer systems.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
authoritative_references.supports: External content can cause indirect prompt injection; OWASP recommends segregating untrusted content, least privilege, approvals, and adversarial testing.

authoritative_references.title: GitHub Advisory GHSA-g8r9-g2v8-jv6f
authoritative_references.supports: A patched Copilot CLI command-safety flaw could turn attacker-influenced repository, MCP, or user content into arbitrary command execution.

revisions.reason: The durable claim is that externally influenced context is an indirect prompt-injection surface for tool-using coding agents. The clip’s specific 9.6 CVSS and normal-PRD account do not match the current GitHub-reviewed Copilot CLI advisory, which rates the verified issue 7.5 and describes crafted command expansion; those details are excluded.

The malicious formatting-template example is an indirect prompt-injection pattern. Isolation and review are directionally useful, while the candidate adds enforceable privilege boundaries, approvals, patching, and adversarial tests.

practices.title: Enforce API object and property response boundaries
practices.statement: Define allowlisted response schemas per operation and audience, enforce server-side authorization for both the requested object and exposed properties, return only necessary fields, validate serialized responses, and test cross-user and sensitive-field denial paths; use non-sequential identifiers only as defense in depth, never as a substitute for authorization.

applicability.description: Internal, partner, public, REST, GraphQL, or RPC APIs that expose application data.
signals: generic model serialization, sensitive or internal fields in responses, client-side filtering, or object identifiers accepted without ownership checks

authoritative_references.title: OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization
authoritative_references.supports: Every API operation that accepts an object identifier must verify the caller's permission for the requested action; identifier format alone does not provide authorization.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
authoritative_references.supports: APIs should cherry-pick authorized properties, enforce schema-based responses, and keep returned data to the minimum required instead of serializing whole backend objects.

revisions.reason: The clip correctly identifies excessive response data and enumerable-object access as API risks. The candidate separates field minimization, property authorization, object authorization, schema enforcement, and tests, and corrects the implication that sequential IDs alone cause unauthorized access.

practices.title: Protect authentication and recovery from abuse
practices.statement: Apply server-side throttling and safe recovery/enumeration behavior using more than IP alone when the threat and traffic model require it.

applicability.description: Applications with login, signup, password reset, or account recovery.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Authentication throttling, safe messages, and recovery-related controls.

authoritative_references.title: Cloudflare Rate Limiting Best Practices
authoritative_references.supports: Documents rate limiting for login endpoints and credential stuffing, with configurable counting characteristics and progressively stronger actions; examples must be adapted to the application.

revisions.reason: Narrowed IP-only reel advice into multi-signal, server-side abuse protection.

Supports throttling and challenge controls on authentication routes. The existing practice intentionally corrects the clip by retaining server-side controls and multi-signal identification instead of relying only on a per-IP edge threshold.

The clip correctly identifies authentication endpoints as rate-limit targets. The existing practice supplies the missing server-side, account-aware, recovery, enumeration, and traffic-model qualifications.
Recovered current primary-source metadata for the rate-limiting URL already cited by this authentication-abuse revision.

practices.title: Protect browser session credentials
practices.statement: Do not persist browser session identifiers or refresh credentials in script-readable storage when secure cookie or backend-mediated designs are available.

applicability.description: Browser applications with authenticated sessions.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Secure, HttpOnly cookie attributes and browser-storage risks for session material.

revisions.reason: Verified current OWASP session guidance and retained client-model applicability.

practices.title: Protect cookie-authenticated browser APIs from cross-site abuse
practices.statement: For cookie-authenticated browser APIs, allow credentialed CORS only from explicit trusted origins and protect state-changing requests with framework CSRF controls, validated tokens, or equivalent origin-aware defenses; treat SameSite cookies as defense in depth.

applicability.description: Browser-facing APIs that authenticate requests with cookies or other automatically attached credentials.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Recommends framework CSRF protection or validated tokens for state-changing requests, explicit trusted CORS origins for credentialed APIs, and SameSite as defense in depth.

authoritative_references.title: WHATWG Fetch Standard
authoritative_references.supports: Defines CORS behavior and the credential-sensitive treatment of wildcard response headers.

revisions.reason: The clip's practical recommendations at 00:55-01:38 align with current CORS and CSRF guidance. The candidate corrects the video's conflation of cross-origin response reading with request forgery and omits the unsupported claim that restricting every unused method is itself a complete access control.

The clip correctly warns against permissive credentialed CORS, but it overstates CORS as what prevents another site from sending cookie-authenticated requests. CORS chiefly controls cross-origin response access; state-changing cookie-authenticated endpoints still need CSRF defenses.

practices.title: Treat package dependencies as executable supply-chain code
practices.statement: Verify package identity and provenance, review direct and transitive dependencies and lifecycle scripts, use reproducible locked installs, and gate known vulnerabilities according to project risk.

applicability.description: Projects that install third-party packages through npm or comparable package managers.

authoritative_references.title: npm threats and mitigations
authoritative_references.supports: Documents malicious-package, typosquatting, dependency-confusion, and compromised-maintainer threats.

authoritative_references.title: npm scripts
authoritative_references.supports: Documents lifecycle scripts executed during installation and the npm ci lockfile-validation sequence.

authoritative_references.title: npm audit
authoritative_references.supports: Documents dependency-tree vulnerability auditing and CI exit behavior.

revisions.reason: The clip correctly frames dependencies and install scripts as executable supply-chain surfaces. The candidate excludes arbitrary popularity and maintainer-age thresholds, and narrows checksum language to package-manager-supported locked and integrity-verified installs.

The package-manager portion supports verified dependencies, locked installs, and risk-based vulnerability scanning, while the catalog avoids assuming weekly scans or ecosystem tooling alone establishes trust.

The clip independently supports treating packages and transitive code as a supply-chain surface, using locked installs, scanning known vulnerabilities, and minimizing unnecessary dependency exposure. The blanket rule that a custom 20-line utility is safer and the implication that version pinning alone blocks compromised releases are excluded.

The clip supports reviewing direct and transitive dependencies, lockfiles, outdated packages, and known vulnerabilities. The claim that npm audit reveals every known vulnerability in every package and the universal red/yellow triage are excluded because registry advisory coverage and remediation policy are risk-dependent.

The clip directly supports reviewing transitive dependencies for known vulnerabilities and committing a package lockfile for reproducible installs. Its exact dependency and vulnerability counts, claim that npm audit identifies every issue precisely, fixed monthly cadence, safe-update simplification, and assertion that ten minutes separates security from a breach are excluded; cadence and gates must follow project risk and tooling coverage.

The clip supports inventorying direct and transitive packages, reviewing maintenance and deprecation signals, scanning known vulnerabilities, and understanding why each dependency is present before release.

A package being unmaintained for two years does not itself prove a vulnerability, and AI-generated code does not universally ignore all package evidence. Vulnerability feeds are incomplete, maintenance is contextual, and package review must assess provenance, execution, transitive exposure, and project risk.

practices.title: Run scoped dynamic security testing
practices.statement: Run authorized dynamic application security testing against representative non-production environments before material releases and periodically; configure authentication, roles, crawl scope, and scan policy, protect test data, manually validate findings, and route confirmed issues through risk-based remediation rather than treating an automated scan as complete assurance.

applicability.description: Browser applications and HTTP APIs with an environment that can safely receive active scanner traffic.

authoritative_references.title: ZAP Scan Policy
authoritative_references.supports: Active scans must be authorized and scoped; automated scanning finds only some vulnerability classes and manual testing remains necessary.

authoritative_references.title: ZAP Getting Started
authoritative_references.supports: ZAP automated scanning spiders and actively scans targets, while authenticated browser or regression-test exploration improves coverage.

revisions.reason: The clip demonstrates useful pre-release automated dynamic scanning and triage. The retained candidate corrects its claim that ZAP finds what every attacker will find: official ZAP guidance says active scanning finds only certain vulnerability classes, requires explicit authorization, and needs configured scope, roles, and manual testing.

The clip supports beginning with repeatable automated DAST and adding deeper expert assessment when risk warrants it. Tool-ranking, fixed coverage percentages, universal quarterly cadence, and claims that Burp scanning exceeds every automated tool are excluded as unsupported or context-dependent.

The clip supports authorized DAST in a representative non-production environment and continuous security checks in delivery workflows. Its claims that ZAP tests the entire OWASP Top 10, identifies exactly where every vulnerability is, or substitutes for professional penetration testing are excluded because automated scanners have scoped, partial coverage and findings require validation.

practices.title: Operate edge abuse controls as defense in depth
practices.statement: Tune edge rate limits, bot controls, and WAF rules from observed traffic; protect the origin from bypass, test rule behavior, monitor false positives and coverage gaps, and retain application-layer authentication, authorization, and input defenses.

applicability.description: Internet-facing applications placed behind a CDN, reverse proxy, API gateway, or WAF.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Secure Cloud Architecture Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: WAFs as an entry-point defense whose generic rules do not cover every attack type.

authoritative_references.title: Cloudflare: Protect your origin server
authoritative_references.supports: Documents multiple origin-protection controls, including proxied DNS, tunnels, authenticated pulls, and Cloudflare IP allowlisting, together with limitations for each approach.

authoritative_references.title: Cloudflare Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS)
authoritative_references.supports: Explains that Authenticated Origin Pulls authenticate Cloudflare-to-origin traffic so direct requests that bypass Cloudflare protections can be rejected; account-specific certificates provide stricter assurance.

authoritative_references.title: Cloudflare Full (strict) SSL/TLS Mode
authoritative_references.supports: Requires encrypted origin connections and a valid, unexpired certificate matching the hostname, and notes that Authenticated Origin Pulls can additionally ensure origin requests are evaluated through Cloudflare.

authoritative_references.title: Cloudflare rate limiting rules
authoritative_references.supports: Edge request matching, mitigation actions, operational limits, and product availability.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
authoritative_references.supports: Recommends endpoint- and business-specific rate limits plus payload, operation, resource, and provider-spend limits to reduce resource exhaustion and cost abuse.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP WSTG architecture mapping
authoritative_references.supports: WAF coverage limitations and the risk of bypassing a cloud WAF through an exposed origin.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 6585 Additional HTTP Status Codes
authoritative_references.supports: Defines HTTP 429 for rate limiting, permits Retry-After, and deliberately leaves client identification and request-counting strategy to the server rather than prescribing a universal threshold.

revisions.reason: Preserves the useful edge-control guidance while correcting universal thresholds and the claim that custom WAF patterns can block the OWASP Top 10. Edge controls require traffic-specific tuning and remain defense in depth.

Directly supports protecting the origin from proxy bypass and securing the proxy-to-origin hop. The durable practice prefers authenticated origin paths or tunnels where available, not only a mutable provider IP allowlist, and requires testing direct-origin access fails.

At roughly 00:35-01:40 the clip supports putting traffic-aware rate controls and an edge filtering layer ahead of an exposed application. Its blanket implication that a WAF and IP bans alone solve DDoS is not retained; the catalog requires traffic-specific tuning, origin protection, monitoring, and defense in depth.

The clip supports per-user and per-endpoint request-rate awareness as an abuse signal. Its fixed example of 50 requests per second is not retained; thresholds require traffic-specific tuning, false-positive monitoring, and application defenses in depth.

The clip supports layered rate limits and bot controls tuned to product usage rather than a single universal threshold. Its claim that token buckets or sliding windows automatically adapt to system health is inaccurate, and its fixed pricing-tier quotas and implication that bots are universally blocked before rate limiting are excluded.

The clip supports rate-limiting costly and public endpoints. Fixed per-user rates, the claim that legitimate users always make two to five requests per minute, and universal five-minute setup or savings are excluded; identity, endpoint cost, distributed traffic, false positives, and origin controls require system-specific tuning.

The clip supports authenticating costly endpoints, validating request shape and size, and applying identity-aware usage controls before expensive model execution. The universal gateway requirement and fixed tier limits are excluded; edge controls remain defense in depth alongside application enforcement.

The clip supports adding rate limiting to exposed APIs. The absolute claim that one setup prevents bots from hammering an API is excluded; effective abuse controls require identity- and endpoint-aware tuning, origin protection, false-positive monitoring, and application defenses in depth.

The clip supports adding request-rate controls to exposed application paths. Its fixed scenario of one thousand requests per second and implication that a backend automatically solves abuse are excluded; controls require traffic-specific tuning, origin protection, and layered application defenses.
Recovered current primary-source metadata for the five edge-control URLs already cited by these source revisions; the references preserve the practice as layered, system-specific defense in depth.

practices.title: Separate public errors from protected diagnostic logs
practices.statement: Return generic, useful errors at external boundaries while recording sufficient server-side diagnostic context for investigation; sanitize untrusted fields, exclude or redact secrets and sensitive identifiers, restrict log access, and test boundary failure paths.

applicability.description: Applications with user-facing, API, webhook, job, or payment-processing boundaries.
signals: External responses expose stack traces, implementation details, connection strings, or secrets; or failures are not observable in protected logs.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Directs REST APIs to return generic errors and avoid unnecessarily revealing failure details.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Defines application logging design, verification, sanitization, sensitive-data exclusions, and access protections.

revisions.reason: The source supports separating user-visible errors from server diagnostics and testing failure paths. The retained claim narrows its unsafe instruction to log every input by requiring sanitization and exclusion or redaction of secrets and sensitive identifiers.

At 00:38-01:11 the clip directly supports generic external errors and detailed protected backend logs. The catalog retains the necessary sanitization, redaction, access-control, and testing qualifications that the clip omits.

The clip directly supports designing unhappy paths, useful user-facing failure states, and investigation records instead of default white screens, stack traces, or opaque 500 responses. Its claim that users spend most of their life on failure paths is rhetorical and excluded.

practices.title: Set browser security headers from a tested policy
practices.statement: Define and test security response headers appropriate to each browser-facing route, including a restrictive Content Security Policy, transport and content-type protections, and framing controls; roll out risky policy changes with reporting and compatibility checks rather than copying a universal header set.

applicability.description: Browser-facing web applications and responses that render or influence active content.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Content Security Policy Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Describes CSP as defense in depth, recommends restrictive policies, and documents report-only delivery as a non-blocking precursor that can reveal violations before enforcement.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP HTTP Security Response Headers Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Describes context-specific browser response headers, recommended values, and limitations such as preferring CSP frame-ancestors over X-Frame-Options where supported.

revisions.reason: At 01:20-01:45 the clip recommends CSP, framing controls, and HSTS. The retained practice corrects its implication that the same headers belong on every response and requires route-appropriate policy, staged rollout, and tests.
The transcript and captions align with current OWASP guidance on resource restriction and staged CSP rollout; the claim that CSP alone stops every compromised-CDN scenario is not generalized.

The clip supports deploying CSP as browser defense in depth. Its claim that CSP completely blocks execution after any injected script tag and that five minutes of configuration removes an entire attack category is excluded; policy must be restrictive, route-aware, compatible, tested, and paired with primary injection defenses.
Recovered current primary-source metadata for the CSP URL already cited by this response-header revision.

practices.title: Validate untrusted input at trusted boundaries
practices.statement: Validate all untrusted inputs at the server-side boundary for expected type, structure, length, range, and business meaning; prefer allowlists where feasible, reject malformed input safely, and still use context-specific parameterization or output encoding because validation alone does not prevent injection.

applicability.description: Endpoints, forms, query parameters, files, messages, and integration feeds that accept data outside the application trust boundary.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Requires early validation of all potentially untrusted inputs at syntactic and semantic levels, preferably server-side and with allowlists.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Treats parameterization and context-specific defenses as primary injection controls, with input validation as an additional layer.

revisions.reason: At 01:48-02:18 the clip recommends validating every endpoint input rather than only form fields. The durable practice adds semantic checks and preserves parameterization or output encoding, correcting the clip’s implication that validation libraries alone stop SQL injection and XSS.

The clip directly supports route-level server-side schema validation before business logic and rejecting malformed input. Its blanket string-sanitization framing is narrowed: validation does not replace context-specific output encoding or parameterized queries, and unexpected fields should follow the API contract rather than always being silently stripped.

The clip directly supports repeating security-relevant input validation at the server boundary even when client-side validation exists. The catalog retains syntactic and semantic validation plus context-specific injection defenses.

The visual checklist correctly states that client-side Zod validation is a UX control, not a security boundary, and calls for server-side validation on write routes. The catalog retains semantic checks and context-specific injection defenses rather than implying one unvalidated route necessarily bypasses every frontend validator.

The clip directly supports server-side validation before trusting malformed or manipulated client data. Its claim that every direct frontend database call necessarily has no validation is excluded; data-layer policies and constraints may be trusted boundaries when correctly configured.

practices.title: Validate JWTs against an application-owned profile
practices.statement: Allowlist acceptable algorithms and bind each key to one algorithm; require all cryptographic checks, validate issuer, audience, token purpose, and required time claims, and use short-lived least-privileged access tokens with protected refresh-token rotation or sender constraint where applicable.

applicability.description: Applications that issue or accept JWTs for authentication, authorization, or inter-service trust.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 8725 JSON Web Token Best Current Practices
authoritative_references.supports: JWT libraries and applications must restrict algorithms, bind keys to one algorithm, validate all cryptographic operations, and validate issuer, audience, and token kind as applicable.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 7519 JSON Web Token
authoritative_references.supports: Defines the exp claim and requires rejecting a token on or after its expiration when the claim is present.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
authoritative_references.supports: Short-lived reduced-scope access tokens limit leakage impact; refresh tokens require risk-based issuance and replay protection through sender constraint or rotation for public clients.

revisions.reason: The clip correctly identifies historical none-algorithm and RSA/HMAC confusion attacks and the need for bounded token lifetimes. The candidate broadens validation to the full application-owned token profile required by current JWT and OAuth guidance; none is not universally forbidden when explicitly selected in a separately protected context, and refresh tokens are not a standalone universal fix.

practices.title: Treat mobile wrappers as native security surfaces
practices.statement: Use platform secret storage, safe claimed links, system TLS validation, and authorization code with PKCE for native OAuth; do not embed backend secrets.

applicability.description: Native or hybrid mobile applications using authentication or deep links.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 8252: OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps
authoritative_references.supports: Native redirect and PKCE requirements.

authoritative_references.title: Android Keystore System
authoritative_references.supports: Provides app-scoped storage for cryptographic keys and credentials, keeps key material non-exportable, and can enforce key-use restrictions outside the application process.

authoritative_references.title: Android security with network protocols
authoritative_references.supports: TLS behavior and cautions about certificate pinning.

authoritative_references.title: Android: Verify App Links
authoritative_references.supports: Documents verified App Links using manifest intent filters and a matching Digital Asset Links file, along with commands for testing domain-verification state.

authoritative_references.title: Apple Keychain Services
authoritative_references.supports: Provides an encrypted keychain database for securely storing small user secrets, cryptographic keys, certificates, and other confidential items.

authoritative_references.title: Apple: Supporting Associated Domains
authoritative_references.supports: Documents the secure website-app association used by universal links and requires matching app entitlements plus an HTTPS apple-app-site-association file.

revisions.reason: Verified PKCE and narrowed blanket certificate-pinning advice.

The clip supports platform secure storage, but prescribes certificate pinning and field-level payload encryption as universal requirements. The catalog deliberately requires system TLS validation and treats pinning as contextual because rotation, trust anchors, and client threat models vary.
The clip independently supports treating a Capacitor wrapper as a native security surface, using platform-protected secret storage, and validating deep-link ownership for authentication flows.

The clip prescribes certificate pinning for every API endpoint and implies ordinary proxies can otherwise intercept valid TLS. Current platform guidance treats pinning as contextual and warns about rotation and trust-anchor failures.

The clip independently supports using platform-claimed HTTPS links backed by site-association files and providing a web fallback for users without the app. Claims that links always open the app, that both platforms need identical configuration, and that one framework configuration universally handles fallback are excluded because verification, manifests, user settings, routing, and platform behavior must be tested.
Recovered current platform-documentation metadata for the four mobile-security URLs already cited by these wrapper and claimed-link source revisions.

practices.title: Preserve authorization and trust boundaries through RAG
practices.statement: Carry source authorization metadata to chunks, enforce the requester's permissions during retrieval, revalidate sources before disclosure, and treat retrieved or uploaded content as untrusted data rather than instructions.

applicability.description: Retrieval-augmented generation systems that ingest private, tenant-scoped, or user-controlled documents.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP RAG Security Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Requires access-control metadata on vector chunks, authorization at retrieval, and treating retrieved content as data rather than commands.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP LLM01 Prompt Injection
authoritative_references.supports: Describes indirect injection through RAG content and recommends privilege restriction, untrusted-content segregation, filtering, and adversarial testing.

revisions.reason: At 00:36-02:21 the clip identifies cross-tenant retrieval leakage and indirect prompt injection, then recommends ownership metadata, permission-filtered retrieval, and a final authorization check. Current OWASP guidance supports those boundaries. The candidate does not claim pattern scanning alone can eliminate prompt injection.

practices.title: Use request signing only for clients that can protect keys
practices.statement: HTTP message signing may protect trusted server-to-server traffic, but is not a universal browser/mobile mutation requirement and needs replay controls.

applicability.description: Trusted service-to-service clients where origin and message integrity justify signing.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures
authoritative_references.supports: Standard signature components and replay-related metadata.

revisions.reason: Replaced a universal HMAC prescription with client-model-specific guidance.

The clip prescribes a shared-secret HMAC for every mutating endpoint. That is unsafe as a universal rule because browsers and other public clients cannot protect a shared secret, signatures do not replace authentication or authorization, and replay controls are also required.

practices.title: Keep secrets out of source and rotate exposures
practices.statement: Keep plaintext credentials out of source code and version history; inject them at runtime through a project-appropriate secret store or protected configuration, scan commits and history for leaks, block supported secrets before push, and promptly revoke or rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

applicability.description: Repositories and delivery pipelines that use API keys, database credentials, tokens, certificates, or other machine secrets.
signals: Credential literal or secret-bearing configuration committed to source control
Leaked credential removed without revocation or rotation
No repository or pipeline secret scanning

authoritative_references.title: GITHUB SECRET SCANNING
authoritative_references.supports: Secret scanning checks Git history for hardcoded credentials, and GitHub directs users to rotate affected credentials immediately.

authoritative_references.title: OWASP SECRETS MANAGEMENT CHEAT SHEET
authoritative_references.supports: Secrets require controlled storage, least privilege, detection, rotation, revocation, and lifecycle management; environment variables are not universally the safest storage mechanism.

revisions.reason: The clip supplies a reusable prevention-and-response kernel: remove secrets from tracked source, scan the full repository history, rotate or revoke exposures, and add pre-push protection. The catalog statement generalizes storage beyond .env files because primary guidance favors purpose-built secret management where practical. practices.title: Audit sensitive state-changing actions
practices.statement: Record purpose-defined audit events for security- and business-sensitive state changes with the authenticated actor, target resource, action, outcome, timestamp, and correlation context; protect the trail from unauthorized access or tampering, exclude secrets and unnecessary personal data, and test that critical events are emitted.

practices.title: Manage authenticated sessions through their full lifecycle
practices.statement: Define risk-appropriate idle and absolute session limits and reauthentication rules; enforce expiration and logout server-side; rotate or invalidate session credentials after authentication, privilege, password, recovery, or compromise events; provide rapid revocation; and test multi-device and federated-session behavior without assuming one universal concurrent-session cap.

applicability.description: Applications that maintain authenticated browser, mobile, API, or federated sessions.
signals: long-lived sessions, reusable refresh tokens, password changes that leave existing sessions active, or no way to revoke a lost device

authoritative_references.title: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet
authoritative_references.supports: Applications should enforce server-side idle and absolute expiration, regenerate session identifiers after privilege changes including password changes, and support termination after risk events.

authoritative_references.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Session Management
authoritative_references.supports: Authenticated sessions require documented inactivity and overall timeouts selected from assurance, endpoint, environment, and application risk, with termination or reauthentication when limits or risk signals require it.

authoritative_references.title: RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
authoritative_references.supports: Short-lived reduced-scope access tokens limit leakage impact; refresh tokens require risk-based issuance and replay protection through sender constraint or rotation for public clients.

practices.title: Give service workloads explicit, rotatable identities
